description: Bundled knowledge for the RAG guidance: why each rule matters and a hand-written vulnerable/fixed example pair per rule.

SEC001.why: eval/exec run text as Python code, so attacker-controlled text becomes attacker-controlled code with the server's privileges.

SEC002.why: A shell interprets ; | & $() and backticks, so text spliced into a command line can append arbitrary commands.

SEC003.why: Credentials in source code are copied to every clone, backup and log of the repository and cannot be rotated without a code change.

SEC004.why: MD5 and SHA-1 have practical collisions and are fast to brute-force, so they do not protect integrity or stored passwords.

SEC005.why: Quotes in user input change the structure of an SQL statement built by concatenation; parameters keep data separate from the query.

SEC006.why: A bare except also catches SystemExit and KeyboardInterrupt and hides real failures, including failed security checks.

SEC007.why: A mutable default is created once and shared by every call, so data leaks between unrelated callers.
SEC007.fixed:
def collect_tags_safe(item, tags=None):
    tags = list(tags or [])
    tags.append(item)
    return tags

SEC008.why: assert statements are removed when Python runs with -O, so a security check written as an assert disappears in production.

SEC009.why: Unpickling runs constructors chosen by the data (__reduce__), so loading untrusted pickle data executes attacker code.

SEC010.why: yaml.load with the full loader can construct arbitrary Python objects from tags in the document.

SEC011.why: The random module is a predictable Mersenne Twister; tokens, passwords and session ids made with it can be predicted.

SEC012.why: Hard-coded addresses tie code to one environment and expose internal network layout.

SEC013.why: '../' sequences or absolute paths in user input escape the intended directory and read or overwrite other files.

SEC014.why: Unescaped user input in HTML runs as script in other users' browsers (cross-site scripting).

SEC015.why: Compiling user input as a Jinja template gives access to Python objects through template expressions ({{ ''.__class__ }}).

SEC016.why: When request data chooses the host of an outbound request, the server can be made to call internal services or cloud metadata endpoints.

SEC017.why: Redirecting to a user-supplied URL lets attackers send victims from a trusted domain to a phishing site.

SEC018.why: External entities in XML can read local files or call internal URLs when the parser resolves them.

SEC019.why: Characters such as * ( ) | & change the meaning of an LDAP filter, so input can widen a search or bypass a login check.

SEC020.why: Quotes and brackets in user input change an XPath expression the same way SQL injection changes a query.

SEC021.why: A JSON body can carry MongoDB operators ($ne, $gt, $where) instead of plain values and turn an equality check into 'match anything'.

SEC022.why: CR/LF in logged input forges extra log lines, hiding attacks or misleading the people who read the logs.

SEC023.why: CR/LF in a header value ends the header and lets the attacker add headers or a body (response splitting).

SEC024.why: A user-supplied regular expression can take exponential time on crafted input (ReDoS) and match far more than intended.

SEC025.why: Importing a module named by the user runs that module's top-level code, which can be any installed module.

SEC026.why: A user-controlled format template can read attributes of the arguments ({0.__class__.__init__.__globals__}) and leak secrets.

SEC027.why: setattr with user-chosen names lets a request overwrite fields it should not (is_admin, owner, price).

SEC028.why: Unvalidated request data in the session is later trusted as if the server had produced it.

SEC029.why: The Werkzeug debugger shows source and lets anyone who reaches it run Python code on the server.

SEC030.why: Without certificate verification any machine on the network path can impersonate the server (man in the middle).

SEC031.why: An unverified SSL context accepts any certificate, so TLS no longer authenticates the server.

SEC032.why: SSLv3, TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 have known protocol attacks (POODLE, BEAST) and are disabled by modern clients.

SEC033.why: DES, 3DES, RC4, RC2 and Blowfish have small keys or blocks or known biases; ciphertexts can be broken or distinguished.
SEC033.vulnerable:
def encrypt_record(key, data):
    return DES.new(key, DES.MODE_CBC).encrypt(data)
SEC033.fixed:
def encrypt_record_safe(key, data):
    return AES.new(key, AES.MODE_GCM).encrypt(data)

SEC034.why: ECB encrypts equal blocks to equal ciphertext, so patterns in the plaintext stay visible.
SEC034.vulnerable:
def encrypt_block(key, data):
    return AES.new(key, AES.MODE_ECB).encrypt(data)
SEC034.fixed:
def encrypt_block_safe(key, data):
    return AES.new(key, AES.MODE_GCM).encrypt(data)

SEC035.why: RSA/DSA keys below 2048 bits can be factored or broken with available computing power.

SEC036.why: Reusing an IV or nonce leaks relationships between messages; for CTR/GCM it reveals plaintext and allows forgery.

SEC037.why: mktemp returns a name without creating the file, so another process can create it first (race / symlink attack).

SEC038.why: World-writable files can be changed by any local user, including code and configuration the application trusts.

SEC039.why: Binding to 0.0.0.0 exposes a service on every network interface, including public ones.

SEC040.why: FTP, Telnet, POP3 and IMAP send credentials and data unencrypted.

SEC041.why: Plain HTTP can be read and modified by anyone on the network path.

SEC042.why: Tar member names with ../ or absolute paths, and links, write files outside the extraction directory.

SEC043.why: With auto-escaping off, every variable rendered into HTML must be escaped by hand; one miss is XSS.

SEC044.why: Cookies without Secure travel over plain HTTP; without HttpOnly they can be read by injected scripts.

SEC045.why: Without CSRF tokens another site can make a logged-in user's browser submit state-changing requests.

SEC046.why: Allowing any origin lets every website read responses meant for the application's own pages.

SEC047.why: Decoding a JWT without verifying its signature trusts claims anyone can write (user id, role).
SEC047.vulnerable:
def read_claims(token):
    return jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False})
SEC047.fixed:
def read_claims_safe(token, key):
    return jwt.decode(token, key, algorithms=["HS256"])

SEC048.why: Accepting unknown SSH host keys lets a man in the middle impersonate the server on the first connection.
SEC048.vulnerable:
def open_ssh(host):
    client = paramiko.SSHClient()
    client.set_missing_host_key_policy(paramiko.AutoAddPolicy())
    client.connect(host)
    return client
SEC048.fixed:
def open_ssh_safe(host):
    client = paramiko.SSHClient()
    client.load_system_host_keys()
    client.set_missing_host_key_policy(paramiko.RejectPolicy())
    client.connect(host)
    return client

SEC049.why: An empty except hides failures, so an error in a security check silently lets the operation continue.

SEC050.why: Logs are kept long, copied widely and read by many people; passwords and tokens in them are effectively disclosed.
SEC050.vulnerable:
def audit_login(username, password):
    logger.info("login attempt %s %s", username, password)
SEC050.fixed:
def audit_login_safe(username, password):
    logger.info("login attempt %s (password length %d)", username, len(password))
